lessons.lessonTitle: What Scientists Actually Do (It's Not a Checklist)
topics: Why science is iterative, not linear
lessons.examTip: Students write hypotheses as questions — a hypothesis must be a TESTABLE STATEMENT in 'if...then...' form; 'Does sunlight affect plant growth?' is a question, not a hypothesis; 'If a plant receives more sunlight, then it will grow taller' is a testable prediction

lessons.lessonTitle: The Difference Between a Good Experiment and a Guess
topics: Independent variable (what you change), dependent variable (what you measure)
Why you can only change ONE variable at a time
lessons.examTip: Students confuse the control group with the controlled variables — the CONTROL GROUP is the untreated baseline for comparison; CONTROLLED VARIABLES are factors kept constant throughout; both are required for a valid experiment

lessons.lessonTitle: How Scientists Measure Things Accurately
topics: Metric system: kilo-, centi-, milli-, conversions
lessons.examTip: Students use 'accurate' and 'precise' as synonyms — a dartboard analogy clarifies it: precise = clustered together (reproducible); accurate = close to the bullseye (correct); you can be precise and wrong, or accurate but inconsistent

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Read Data and Tell If It Supports Your Hypothesis
topics: Tables vs. graphs: when to use which
Interpreting line graphs: trends and outliers
Correlation: patterns in data without claiming cause
lessons.examTip: Students say data 'proves' a hypothesis — science never proves; data SUPPORTS or REFUTES a hypothesis; the correct language is 'the data is consistent with' or 'the data does not support'; one experiment never gives final proof

lessons.lessonTitle: What Matter Is Made Of and How We Know
topics: States of matter and particle motion
lessons.examTip: Students confuse compounds and mixtures — in a COMPOUND, elements are chemically bonded in fixed ratios (water is always H₂O); in a MIXTURE, substances are physically combined and can be separated without a chemical reaction

lessons.lessonTitle: What a Chemical Reaction Is (and Isn't)
topics: Signs of a chemical reaction: gas, precipitate, color change, heat
lessons.examTip: Students say ice melting is a chemical change because 'it looks different' — a physical change alters form but NOT chemical identity; melting, dissolving, and cutting are physical; burning, rusting, and digesting are chemical; the substance identity either changes or it doesn't

lessons.lessonTitle: How Forces Change Motion (Newton's Laws in Plain Language)
topics: Force, mass, and acceleration: F = ma concept
Friction and gravity as everyday forces
lessons.examTip: Students say an object moving at constant speed has no forces on it — constant speed means forces are BALANCED (net force = 0), not absent; a car cruising requires engine force to balance friction; zero net force ≠ no forces

lessons.lessonTitle: What Energy Is and Why It Can't Disappear
lessons.examTip: Students say energy is 'lost' in a system — energy is TRANSFORMED, not destroyed; a roller coaster converts PE to KE to heat (friction); 'lost' energy became thermal energy; asking where the energy WENT is the correct scientific framing

lessons.lessonTitle: What Makes Something Alive
topics: Seven characteristics of life: MRS GREN
Cell as basic unit of life
lessons.examTip: Students say fire and cars are alive because they grow and use energy — life requires ALL characteristics (reproduction, response to environment, homeostasis, cells); fire lacks cells and cannot reproduce; applying all criteria simultaneously is essential

lessons.lessonTitle: How Cells Get Energy: The Short Version
topics: Photosynthesis: light + CO₂ + water → glucose + oxygen
Cellular respiration: glucose + oxygen → CO₂ + water + energy
Why both processes are essential to life on Earth
lessons.examTip: Students say only plants do photosynthesis and only animals do respiration — ALL living cells perform cellular respiration; plants do BOTH photosynthesis AND respiration; in darkness, a plant only respires and actually releases CO₂

lessons.lessonTitle: How Traits Are Passed From Parents to Offspring
lessons.examTip: Students say a dominant trait is more common in a population — dominant means it's expressed when present, NOT that it's more frequent; a dominant disease allele can be rare; frequency in a population has nothing to do with dominance

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Living Things Are Classified Into Groups
lessons.examTip: Students write binomial nomenclature with both words capitalized — only the GENUS is capitalized; the species epithet is lowercase: Homo sapiens, not Homo Sapiens; when handwritten, both words are underlined; when typed, both are italicized

lessons.lessonTitle: What the Rock Cycle Tells Us About Earth's History
topics: Three rock types: igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic
How each type forms and transforms
Reading rock layers (strata) as a timeline
lessons.examTip: Students say rocks always follow the cycle in one direction — the rock cycle has NO fixed order; igneous rock can become metamorphic directly under heat/pressure without becoming sedimentary first; arrows go multiple directions

lessons.lessonTitle: How Plate Tectonics Explains Earthquakes, Volcanoes, and Mountains
topics: Evidence for plate tectonics: seafloor spreading, fossil distribution
Why plate boundaries are where action happens
lessons.examTip: Students say earthquakes only occur at plate boundaries — MOST earthquakes occur at boundaries, but intraplate earthquakes exist; the New Madrid Seismic Zone in the US interior is a tested example; 'most' and 'only' are different claims

lessons.lessonTitle: What Weather vs. Climate Actually Means
topics: Weather = short-term atmospheric conditions; climate = long-term patterns
Factors affecting climate: latitude, altitude, ocean currents
Why 'it's cold today' doesn't disprove climate change
lessons.examTip: Students use weather events as evidence for or against climate change — weather is day-to-day; climate is 30+ year patterns; a cold snap is a weather event; climate change refers to shifts in the GLOBAL AVERAGE over decades, not individual days

lessons.lessonTitle: The Building Blocks: Points, Lines, and Planes Have Rules
lessons.examTip: Students treat a postulate and a theorem as the same thing — a POSTULATE is assumed true without proof (a starting rule); a THEOREM is proved using postulates and other theorems; the difference matters when writing proofs

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Write a Two-Column Proof Without Getting Stuck
topics: Common reasons: given, definition, postulate, theorem
lessons.examTip: Students write 'because it looks equal' or 'obvious' as reasons — every reason must be a named DEFINITION, POSTULATE, or THEOREM; acceptable reasons are formal mathematical names; informal observations earn no credit in a proof

lessons.lessonTitle: What Congruence Actually Means (Not Just 'Same Size')
topics: Congruent segments and angles: exact same measure
lessons.examTip: Students write AB = CD when they mean AB ≅ CD — segments and angles are CONGRUENT (≅); their MEASURES are equal (=); 'AB = CD' means the lengths are equal numbers; '∠A = ∠B' should be '∠A ≅ ∠B' unless referring to degree measures

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Triangles Always Add Up to 180° (and How to Use That)
topics: Finding missing angles in multi-triangle figures
lessons.examTip: Students apply the 180° rule to quadrilaterals — the interior angle sum is 180° only for TRIANGLES; for any polygon, sum = (n−2) × 180°; a quadrilateral sums to 360°, not 180°

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Prove Two Triangles Are Congruent (All Five Shortcuts)
topics: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, HL congruence shortcuts
Why SSA and AAA do NOT guarantee congruence
CPCTC as a reason after proving congruence
lessons.examTip: Students use SSA (Side-Side-Angle) as a congruence shortcut — SSA is NOT valid and can produce two different triangles (the ambiguous case); HL (Hypotenuse-Leg) is valid ONLY for right triangles; SSA for non-right triangles does not prove congruence

lessons.lessonTitle: What's Special About Isosceles and Equilateral Triangles
topics: Isosceles triangle theorem: base angles are equal
Converse: equal angles means equal sides
lessons.examTip: Students identify the 'base' of an isosceles triangle as the bottom side regardless of orientation — the BASE is the NON-EQUAL side (between the two equal sides); the figure can be rotated; always identify which two sides are equal first

lessons.lessonTitle: How the Pythagorean Theorem Works and When to Use It
topics: a² + b² = c² where c is the hypotenuse
Converse: if a²+b²=c², then it's a right triangle
lessons.examTip: Students assign c to any side — c is ALWAYS the hypotenuse (the longest side, opposite the right angle); assigning c to a leg and solving gives a wrong answer every time; identify the right angle first, then c is the side opposite it

lessons.lessonTitle: Special Right Triangles: The Two Shortcuts Worth Memorizing
topics: 30-60-90: short leg = x, long leg = x√3, hypotenuse = 2x
lessons.examTip: Students multiply the SHORT leg by 2 to get the hypotenuse in a 30-60-90 — this is correct ONLY when the SHORT LEG is x; if given the hypotenuse or long leg, divide first to find x, then multiply; starting from the wrong side cascades into wrong answers

lessons.lessonTitle: The Hierarchy of Quadrilaterals (Every Square Is a Rectangle — Not Vice Versa)
lessons.examTip: Students say 'a rectangle is a square' — a square IS a rectangle (all squares have 4 right angles) but a rectangle is NOT necessarily a square (it doesn't need equal sides); the hierarchy flows one way; Venn diagram thinking prevents this error

lessons.lessonTitle: What Parallelogram Properties Let You Solve Problems
topics: Opposite sides equal and parallel; opposite angles equal
lessons.examTip: Students say diagonals of a parallelogram are equal — diagonals bisect each other in ALL parallelograms, but they are only EQUAL in a rectangle; only PERPENDICULAR in a rhombus; only BOTH in a square; don't over-apply properties

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Find Interior and Exterior Angles of Any Polygon
topics: Each interior angle of regular polygon = (n−2)×180°/n
Each exterior angle of regular polygon = 360°/n
lessons.examTip: Students confuse interior and exterior angle formulas — for a REGULAR polygon: each EXTERIOR angle = 360°/n (always); each INTERIOR angle = 180° − exterior angle; students frequently apply the 360°/n formula to find interior angles, getting the wrong answer

lessons.lessonTitle: All the Parts of a Circle and What They're Called
lessons.examTip: Students confuse arc MEASURE (in degrees) and arc LENGTH (in linear units) — arc measure equals the central angle in degrees; arc length = (arc measure/360) × 2πr; these require different formulas and are frequently mixed up

lessons.lessonTitle: The Inscribed Angle Theorem: Half the Central Angle
topics: Inscribed angle = half the intercepted arc
Two inscribed angles intercepting the same arc are equal
lessons.examTip: Students set inscribed angle equal to the arc instead of half the arc — the inscribed angle is HALF the intercepted arc; the central angle EQUALS the intercepted arc; confusing which is which produces exactly the wrong answer

lessons.lessonTitle: How Tangent Lines and the Radius Are Always Related
topics: Tangent perpendicular to radius at point of tangency
Two tangents from external point are equal length
lessons.examTip: Students forget the 90° angle at the point of tangency — when a tangent meets a radius, they form a RIGHT ANGLE; this creates right triangles in problems where none seem obvious; most tangent-line problems are secretly Pythagorean theorem problems

lessons.lessonTitle: How Distance and Midpoint Formulas Come From Pythagorean Theorem
lessons.examTip: Students average the x-coordinates but subtract the y-coordinates in midpoint (or vice versa) — midpoint takes the AVERAGE of BOTH x AND y; both coordinates use the same averaging operation; students sometimes apply the distance formula operation to midpoint

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Prove a Shape Is What You Say It Is Using Coordinates
topics: Proving parallelogram: equal and parallel opposite sides
Proving rectangle: perpendicular adjacent sides (slopes are negative reciprocals)
lessons.examTip: Students prove a rectangle by showing all four sides equal — equal sides proves a RHOMBUS, not a rectangle; to prove rectangle, show right angles using PERPENDICULAR SLOPES (negative reciprocal slopes); these two proofs are completely different

lessons.lessonTitle: What the Equation of a Circle Means Geometrically
topics: Identifying center (h,k) and radius from equation
Completing the square to convert general form
lessons.examTip: Students read center from (x−h)²+(y−k)²=r² as (−h, −k) — the center is (h, k) with the OPPOSITE signs of what appears in the equation; (x−3)²+(y+2)²=25 has center (3, −2), not (−3, 2); the sign flip is the same trap as vertex form of a parabola

lessons.lessonTitle: How Surface Area and Volume Are Different Problems
topics: Surface area: sum of all face areas
Units: SA in square units, V in cubic units
lessons.examTip: Students use volume formula when asked for surface area (and vice versa) — SURFACE AREA measures the OUTSIDE wrapping (square units); VOLUME measures what it holds (cubic units); re-read the question to identify which is asked before selecting a formula

lessons.lessonTitle: The Formula Patterns for Prisms, Cylinders, Pyramids, and Cones
lessons.examTip: Students forget the ⅓ in pyramid and cone volume — pyramids and cones hold EXACTLY one-third the volume of the corresponding prism or cylinder with the same base and height; physically, three conical fills equal one cylinder; forgetting this gives volume 3× too large

lessons.lessonTitle: How Scale Factor Changes Size, Area, and Volume
topics: Linear scale factor k: lengths multiply by k
lessons.examTip: Students apply the linear scale factor to area and volume — if a figure is scaled by k, LENGTHS multiply by k, AREAS by k², VOLUMES by k³; doubling all dimensions of a box makes it 8× the volume (2³), not 2× or 4×; students consistently under-apply the exponent

lessons.lessonTitle: What a Variable Actually Means (And Why x Isn't Scary)
topics: Variable as a placeholder for an unknown number
Difference between an expression and an equation
lessons.examTip: Students add variables and numbers: 3x + 4 = 7x — you CANNOT combine 3x and 4 because they are unlike terms (different kinds); 3x + 4 is already fully simplified; only LIKE TERMS (same variable, same exponent) can be combined

lessons.lessonTitle: The Order of Operations Is Not Optional
topics: Common mistakes with subtraction and division
lessons.examTip: Students do addition before subtraction because 'A comes before S' in PEMDAS — addition and subtraction have EQUAL priority; work LEFT TO RIGHT; 10 − 3 + 2 = 9 (not 5); the same applies to multiplication and division

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Combine Like Terms Without Losing Anything
topics: Identifying like terms: same variable, same exponent
lessons.examTip: Students distribute only to the first term in parentheses: 3(x + 4) = 3x + 4 — the 3 must multiply EVERY term inside: 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12; forgetting to distribute to the constant is the most common distributive property error

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Solve an Equation by Undoing What Was Done to x
topics: Inverse operations to isolate the variable
lessons.examTip: Students perform operations in PEMDAS order when solving — solving equations reverses PEMDAS; undo addition/subtraction FIRST (outermost operations), then multiplication/division (innermost); doing it in PEMDAS order locks the variable inside instead of isolating it

lessons.lessonTitle: What Happens When You Solve an Equation With Variables on Both Sides
topics: Moving all variable terms to one side
Combining like terms across the equals sign
Equations with no solution or infinitely many solutions
lessons.examTip: Students get 0 = 0 or 5 = 3 and say there's no solution in both cases — 0 = 0 (always true) means INFINITELY MANY solutions (all values work); 5 = 3 (always false) means NO solution; these are opposite conclusions from similar-looking steps

lessons.lessonTitle: The One Rule That Makes Inequalities Different from Equations
topics: Solving inequalities like equations — except one rule
Flip the inequality when multiplying or dividing by a negative
Graphing solutions on a number line: open vs. closed circle
lessons.examTip: Students flip the inequality sign every time they touch a negative number — only flip when MULTIPLYING or DIVIDING both sides by a negative; subtracting a negative (adding) does NOT flip the sign; the sign flip rule is specifically about the operation, not the presence of negatives

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Write and Solve Equations From Word Problems
topics: Defining the variable before writing an equation
Translating verbal phrases to algebraic expressions
Checking that your answer makes sense in context
lessons.examTip: Students define x as 'the problem' rather than a specific quantity — define x precisely: 'let x = the number of apples Sarah bought'; vague definitions lead to equations that solve for the wrong thing; the definition determines what your answer means

lessons.lessonTitle: What Makes a Relationship a Function (The Rule Every Graph Must Follow)
topics: Function: each input has exactly one output
Function notation: f(x) means output when input is x
lessons.examTip: Students say x = 3 is a function because 'it's just a line' — a VERTICAL line fails the vertical line test and is NOT a function; every x must map to exactly one y; x = 3 maps one x-value to infinitely many y-values, violating the definition

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Graph a Line from an Equation Without Making a Table
topics: Plotting y-intercept, then using slope to find next point
Horizontal and vertical lines: y = k and x = h
lessons.examTip: Students plot the slope as a single point instead of a ratio — slope is RISE OVER RUN, meaning 'go up rise units, then right run units'; a slope of 3/4 means up 3 RIGHT 4 from any point; treating slope as just another coordinate to plot gives a random point, not the next point on the line

lessons.lessonTitle: How Domain and Range Describe What a Function Can Do
topics: Restrictions: no division by zero, no square root of negative
lessons.examTip: Students give range as all real numbers for y = x² — the RANGE of y = x² is y ≥ 0 because squaring any real number gives a non-negative result; the graph only exists at and above the x-axis; always consider what output values are actually achievable

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Add, Subtract, and Multiply Polynomials
topics: Combining like terms (same variable, same degree)
Distributing a monomial: multiply each term
lessons.examTip: Students add exponents when adding like terms: x² + x² = x⁴ — adding like terms ADDS the coefficients, not the exponents: x² + x² = 2x²; MULTIPLYING terms adds exponents: x² · x² = x⁴; addition and multiplication are completely different operations

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Factor Out the GCF (The First Thing You Always Try)
topics: Finding the greatest common factor of all terms
Why factoring is the reverse of distributing
lessons.examTip: Students factor out a number that doesn't divide all terms evenly — the GCF must divide INTO every single term; to find it, list the factors of each coefficient and each variable, then pick the highest common value; after factoring, check by distributing back

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Factor a Trinomial x² + bx + c
topics: Finding two numbers that multiply to c and add to b
Signs: when both positive, both negative, or mixed
lessons.examTip: Students guess factors without checking the signs systematically — for x² − 5x + 6: multiply to +6 and add to −5 means BOTH numbers must be negative (−2 × −3 = +6, −2 + −3 = −5); drawing a small table of factor pairs and their sums is faster than guessing

lessons.lessonTitle: What a Parabola's Vertex and Axis of Symmetry Tell You
topics: Opening direction from sign of a
lessons.examTip: Students find the axis of symmetry as −b/a instead of −b/2a — the axis of symmetry formula is x = −b/(2a), where 2a is in the denominator; forgetting the 2 gives an axis that's off by a factor of 2; write the full formula before substituting

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Solve a Quadratic Equation Three Different Ways
topics: Factoring: set each factor = 0 (Zero Product Property)
Square root method: when no bx term
lessons.examTip: Students apply the quadratic formula to every problem before trying to factor — factoring is faster and less error-prone when the quadratic factors nicely; use the discriminant (b²−4ac) first: if it's a perfect square, factor; if not, use the formula

lessons.lessonTitle: What the Discriminant Predicts Before You Solve
lessons.examTip: Students compute the discriminant as b² − 4c (omitting a) — the discriminant is b² − 4AC, where ALL THREE of a, b, and c must be identified from ax² + bx + c = 0; omitting a (or using the unset equation) gives wrong discrimination results

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Find What the Author Is Really Saying
topics: Distinguishing major details from minor ones
lessons.examTip: Students confuse the topic with the main idea — the TOPIC is what it's about ('dogs'); the MAIN IDEA is what the author says about it ('Dogs make better companions than cats because...'); the main idea must be a STATEMENT, not just a label

lessons.lessonTitle: How Authors Use Evidence to Support Their Points
topics: How supporting details connect to the main idea
Evaluating whether evidence is relevant and sufficient
lessons.examTip: Students accept any statement as a fact if it sounds authoritative — a FACT is verifiable and can be proven true or false; an OPINION is a belief or judgment ('this is the best policy'); statements using 'should,' 'best,' 'worst,' or 'I believe' signal opinions

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Infer What the Author Didn't Say Directly
topics: What 'reading between the lines' actually means
Avoiding inferences that go beyond the text
lessons.examTip: Students make inferences that the text doesn't support — a valid inference must be SUPPORTED BY TEXTUAL EVIDENCE; it's not a guess about anything beyond what the text implies; if no evidence points to your inference, it's speculation, not inference

lessons.lessonTitle: How Vocabulary Context Clues Help You Figure Out Unknown Words
topics: Definition context clues: the word is explained nearby
lessons.examTip: Students look up words in their head without checking context — the CONTEXT meaning may differ from the dictionary definition; a word like 'draft' or 'charge' has multiple meanings; always use the surrounding sentences to determine which meaning fits

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Write a Thesis That Actually Takes a Position
topics: Thesis = one arguable claim, not a topic announcement
Where the thesis goes: end of introduction
The difference between a topic sentence and a thesis
lessons.examTip: Students write 'In this essay I will discuss...' as a thesis — this announces a topic, not an argument; a thesis must make a CLAIM that can be agreed with or disagreed with; 'Social media harms teenagers because it disrupts sleep and amplifies anxiety' is a thesis

lessons.lessonTitle: What a Strong Body Paragraph Must Include
topics: Topic sentence that supports the thesis
Commentary explaining what the evidence proves
lessons.examTip: Students end paragraphs after a quote — a quote needs COMMENTARY explaining what it means and how it proves the topic sentence; 'This quote shows...' followed by real explanation; ending with evidence alone leaves the reader to make the connection for you

lessons.lessonTitle: Common Grammar Mistakes That Change Your Meaning
topics: Sentence fragments: missing subject or verb
lessons.examTip: Students fix comma splices by adding a comma before 'however' — 'however' is a conjunctive adverb, not a coordinating conjunction; joining two independent clauses requires either a SEMICOLON before 'however' or a period; 'I tried, however I failed' is still a comma splice

lessons.lessonTitle: How Transitions Connect Ideas (Not Just Fill Space)
topics: Transitions showing addition, contrast, cause-effect, example
Using transitions to signal logical relationships
lessons.examTip: Students start every paragraph with 'Also' or 'Additionally' — these only show ADDITION; use transitions that reflect the actual logical relationship: contrast (however, although), cause-effect (therefore, as a result), emphasis (indeed, above all); 'also' for every paragraph suggests no logical structure

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Identify What a Story Is Really About (Theme vs. Plot)
topics: Plot = what happens; theme = what it means
How multiple elements contribute to theme
lessons.examTip: Students write theme as one word ('friendship') — theme is a SENTENCE that makes a claim: 'True friendship requires accepting someone's flaws, not just their strengths'; the one-word version is a topic, not a theme; always push from the topic word to a full thematic statement

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Analyze a Character as More Than Just Their Traits
topics: How characters are revealed through actions, speech, thoughts
How characters change in response to conflict
lessons.examTip: Students list personality traits rather than analyzing them — describing a character as 'brave' earns no credit; analyzing HOW the author shows bravery through specific actions, what the bravery COSTS the character, and what it REVEALS about the theme is the actual analytical task

lessons.lessonTitle: How Figurative Language Creates Meaning Beyond Literal Words
topics: Simile and metaphor: comparison and what it reveals
Personification: giving human qualities to nonhuman things
Symbolism: objects that represent larger ideas
lessons.examTip: Students identify the device but stop there — 'The author uses a metaphor' earns minimal credit; the analysis must explain WHAT IS BEING COMPARED and WHAT THE COMPARISON REVEALS about the character, mood, or theme; identification is just step one

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Build an Argument That Actually Persuades Someone
topics: Claim supported by reasons and evidence
Why a counterargument makes your argument stronger
lessons.examTip: Students skip the counterargument because they think it weakens their position — addressing the opposing view and REFUTING it shows the reader you've thought carefully; ignoring it makes readers think you haven't considered it; concession + refutation builds credibility

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Use Sources Without Letting Them Take Over
lessons.examTip: Students drop in a quote and move on — every source needs: (1) introduction (who said it and why they're credible), (2) the quote or paraphrase, (3) explanation of what it proves for YOUR argument; skipping the explanation makes the source do all the work for you

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Tell If a Source Is Trustworthy
lessons.examTip: Students accept any website as a source — evaluate AUTHOR expertise (does this person know the subject?), PURPOSE (is it trying to inform or sell/persuade?), and DATE (is it current enough for your topic?); a .org or .edu domain is not an automatic guarantee of accuracy

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Colonists Came to America (And Who Was Already There)
topics: Native American cultures and early contact
Three main colonial regions and their differences
lessons.examTip: Students describe colonization as if America were empty — Native American nations were DISPLACED by colonization, not simply absent; the impact on indigenous peoples (disease, land loss, warfare) must be part of any account of colonial settlement

lessons.lessonTitle: Why the Colonists Decided to Break Away From Britain
topics: Taxation without representation: Stamp Act, Townshend Acts
Boston Massacre and Tea Party as turning points
lessons.examTip: Students say the Revolution was only about taxes — the deeper issue was SELF-GOVERNANCE; colonists had run their own assemblies for decades and saw Parliament's new assertiveness as an attack on rights they already had; taxes were the symptom, not the root cause

lessons.lessonTitle: What the Constitution Set Up and Why It Was Designed That Way
topics: Three branches and separation of powers
Checks and balances: each branch limiting the others
lessons.examTip: Students describe checks and balances as 'three equal branches' — the branches are equal in STATUS but not in every POWER; Congress overrides vetoes (2/3), the president nominates judges, Congress confirms them; each branch has specific powers OVER specific other branches

lessons.lessonTitle: How the North and South Became Two Different Economies
topics: How economic differences created political conflict
lessons.examTip: Students describe slavery as 'just a Southern issue' — slavery was economically connected to the ENTIRE country; Northern textile mills depended on Southern cotton; banks in New York financed plantations; slavery's reach was national, not regional, which made abolition politically explosive

lessons.lessonTitle: What Manifest Destiny Was and Who It Hurt
topics: Idea that westward expansion was America's destiny
Displacement of Native Americans: Indian Removal Act, Trail of Tears
lessons.examTip: Students describe westward expansion only through the pioneers' perspective — a complete answer includes the COST paid by Native American nations and Mexicans; Manifest Destiny required taking land from people already living there; both perspectives must appear in analysis

lessons.lessonTitle: Why the Civil War Was Ultimately About Slavery
topics: States' rights debate centered on slavery specifically
lessons.examTip: Students say the Civil War was 'really about states' rights, not slavery' — the SPECIFIC right being claimed was the right to keep slavery; Confederate documents explicitly name slavery as the cause of secession; 'states' rights' is not a neutral term in this context

lessons.lessonTitle: How Big Business Changed American Life After the Civil War
topics: Carnegie (steel) and Rockefeller (oil): vertical and horizontal integration
lessons.examTip: Students describe big business as purely negative — industrialization created jobs, lowered consumer prices, and connected the nation; the problem was CONCENTRATION OF POWER without accountability; both the benefits and the dangers are required for a complete answer

lessons.lessonTitle: What Immigrants and Workers Did to Shape American Society
topics: New immigration waves from Southern and Eastern Europe
Working conditions: hours, pay, child labor
Labor unions: strikes, collective bargaining, Pullman Strike
lessons.examTip: Students say unions immediately improved conditions — unions faced violent opposition (Homestead Strike, Pullman Strike) and won gains slowly over decades; the government often sided with business owners; early labor movement history is a story of struggle and setback, not quick victory

lessons.lessonTitle: How the Progressive Movement Tried to Fix the Problems of Industry
topics: Muckrakers exposing corruption and unsafe conditions
Limits: Progressivism often excluded Black Americans
lessons.examTip: Students present Progressivism as solving all industrial problems — many Progressive reforms were LIMITED to white Americans; segregation intensified during the Progressive Era (Wilson re-segregated federal buildings); 'progressive' didn't mean equal rights for all

lessons.lessonTitle: How WWI and WWII Made America a World Power
topics: US entry into WWI: Zimmermann Telegram, unrestricted submarine warfare
WWII: from isolation to global war after Pearl Harbor
How wartime production ended the Great Depression
lessons.examTip: Students say the US was always willing to enter both wars — the US maintained ISOLATIONISM until specific events forced entry (Zimmermann Telegram for WWI, Pearl Harbor for WWII); Congress and the public strongly opposed involvement before these events; entry was not inevitable

lessons.lessonTitle: What the Cold War Was (It Wasn't Just About Nuclear Weapons)
topics: Korean War and Vietnam as containment in practice
Space race and arms race as competition beyond military
lessons.examTip: Students say the Cold War was a military conflict between the US and USSR — it was a POLITICAL, ECONOMIC, and IDEOLOGICAL competition that rarely involved direct combat; 'hot' wars in Korea and Vietnam were proxy conflicts; the two superpowers never directly fought each other

lessons.lessonTitle: How the Civil Rights Movement Changed America
topics: Direct action: sit-ins, boycotts, freedom rides
Key legislation: Civil Rights Act 1964, Voting Rights Act 1965
Why legal equality and economic equality are different challenges
lessons.examTip: Students say the Civil Rights Act 'solved' racism — the legislation ended LEGAL discrimination but did not eliminate economic inequality or social racism; the movement's ongoing challenges (poverty, housing discrimination, police violence) show that legal rights and lived equality are different goals

lessons.lessonTitle: Everything Around You Is Matter — Here's How to Describe It
lessons.examTip: Students classify solutions as pure substances because they look uniform — a solution is a HOMOGENEOUS MIXTURE, not a pure substance; saltwater looks uniform but can be separated by evaporation; pure substances (elements and compounds) cannot be physically separated

lessons.lessonTitle: How Scientists Measure Things in Chemistry
topics: SI units: mass (g), volume (mL or L), temperature (K)
Significant figures: what they mean and how to count them
Density: D = m/V and its uses
lessons.examTip: Students count ALL digits as significant — zeros are TRICKY: leading zeros are NOT significant (0.0045 has 2 sig figs); trailing zeros after a decimal ARE significant (2.50 has 3 sig figs); trailing zeros without a decimal are ambiguous; use scientific notation to be clear

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Convert Units Without Getting Confused
lessons.examTip: Students multiply by conversion factors without canceling units — in dimensional analysis, write units in EVERY step and cancel them like fractions; if you can't cancel the unit you want to eliminate, the conversion factor is upside down; units that remain are your answer's units

lessons.lessonTitle: What an Atom Is Made Of and Where Those Parts Are
topics: Protons and neutrons in the nucleus; electrons in orbitals
Atomic number = protons; mass number = protons + neutrons
Ions: gaining or losing electrons changes charge, not identity
lessons.examTip: Students say an ion is a different ELEMENT — gaining or losing electrons changes the CHARGE, not the number of protons; an atom's IDENTITY is determined by proton count (atomic number); Na⁺ is still sodium; only changing protons creates a different element

lessons.lessonTitle: How the Periodic Table Organizes Every Element
topics: Periodic trends: atomic radius, ionization energy, electronegativity
lessons.examTip: Students say ionization energy and atomic radius increase in the same direction — they move in OPPOSITE TRENDS across a period; as you go right, atomic radius DECREASES (more protons pull electrons closer); ionization energy INCREASES (harder to remove electrons held tighter)

lessons.lessonTitle: How Electrons Are Arranged and Why It Matters
topics: Electron configuration: filling order by energy level
lessons.examTip: Students say all elements want to have 8 electrons — the octet rule applies to most main group elements, but EXCEPTIONS exist; hydrogen follows the duet rule (2 electrons); some elements like phosphorus and sulfur can expand beyond 8; hydrogen and helium are the key exceptions

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Read and Write Chemical Equations
topics: Conservation of mass: atoms balanced on both sides
lessons.examTip: Students change subscripts to balance equations — NEVER change subscripts to balance; H₂O₂ ≠ H₂O; subscripts define the substance; only change COEFFICIENTS in front of formulas; changing a subscript creates an entirely different chemical

lessons.lessonTitle: The Five Types of Chemical Reactions and How to Recognize Them
lessons.examTip: Students confuse single and double replacement — SINGLE: one element displaces another in a compound (A + BC → AC + B); DOUBLE: the cations of two compounds switch partners (AB + CD → AD + CB); identifying whether one or two elements are switching determines the type

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Use Moles to Predict How Much Product You Make
lessons.examTip: Students convert grams directly to grams of product — stoichiometry requires going THROUGH MOLES: grams A → moles A → moles B → grams B; skipping the mole conversion and just using a mass ratio gives wrong answers except by coincidence

lessons.lessonTitle: What 'Dissolving' Actually Means at the Particle Level
lessons.examTip: Students say 'water dissolves everything' — water only dissolves POLAR and IONIC substances ('like dissolves like'); oil doesn't dissolve in water because oil is nonpolar; this principle predicts what will dissolve before any experiment is run

lessons.lessonTitle: What Acids and Bases Actually Are
topics: Acids: donate H⁺; bases: accept H⁺ (Brønsted-Lowry)
Strong vs. weak acids: complete vs. partial dissociation
lessons.examTip: Students say a low pH means 'a little acidic' — pH 2 is EXTREMELY acidic; each pH unit represents a 10× change in H⁺ concentration; pH 2 has 100× more H⁺ than pH 4; students confuse the magnitude of the number with the intensity of acidity

lessons.lessonTitle: What Happens When an Acid and a Base Are Mixed
topics: Titration: using a known concentration to find an unknown
lessons.examTip: Students say neutralization means the products are neutral — a neutralization REACTION produces a salt and water, but the resulting solution is not necessarily pH 7; strong acid + weak base → acidic salt; weak acid + strong base → basic salt; the product's pH depends on which reactant is stronger

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Every Living Thing Is Made of Cells
topics: Cell theory: all life made of cells
lessons.examTip: Students say plant cells have all the same organelles as animal cells — plants have CELL WALLS, CHLOROPLASTS, and a LARGE CENTRAL VACUOLE that animal cells lack; animal cells have CENTRIOLES that plant cells lack; the differences are directly tied to each cell's unique functions

lessons.lessonTitle: What Each Organelle Does and Why It Matters
topics: Endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi: protein production line
Chloroplasts and cell wall in plant cells
lessons.examTip: Students say the nucleus makes proteins — the NUCLEUS contains the DNA instructions; RIBOSOMES make proteins using those instructions; the rough ER processes proteins, the Golgi modifies and ships them; this is a multi-step assembly line, not a single organelle job

lessons.lessonTitle: How Materials Get In and Out of Cells
topics: Osmosis effects: crenation and lysis in different solutions
lessons.examTip: Students say a cell placed in salt water will swell — a cell in HIGH SALT (hypertonic) solution loses water by osmosis and SHRINKS (crenation in animal cells, plasmolysis in plant cells); a cell in PURE WATER (hypotonic) gains water and swells; water moves toward MORE solute

lessons.lessonTitle: How Traits Are Inherited From Parents
lessons.examTip: Students say a dominant trait is 'stronger' or 'better' — dominant simply means it's expressed when present; it has NO relationship to being beneficial or common; a harmful dominant allele (like Huntington's disease) is expressed even with one copy

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Predict Offspring Using a Punnett Square
lessons.examTip: Students report Punnett square results as exact numbers instead of probabilities — a 3:1 phenotype ratio means a 75% chance of the dominant phenotype per offspring, not that exactly 3 out of 4 offspring will show it; probability applies to EACH individual offspring, not a guaranteed count

lessons.lessonTitle: How DNA Carries the Instructions for Making You
topics: DNA structure: double helix, base pairing (A-T, G-C)
Gene: section of DNA coding for a protein
DNA replication: copying before cell division
lessons.examTip: Students say A pairs with G and T pairs with C — base pairing is A-T and G-C (in DNA); A pairs with T, not G; G pairs with C, not A; this rule is called complementary base pairing and determines both DNA replication and transcription accuracy

lessons.lessonTitle: What Natural Selection Actually Is (Evolution Explained Simply)
topics: Traits that improve survival are inherited more
Natural selection acts on individuals; evolution happens to populations
lessons.examTip: Students say 'organisms evolve to survive' — organisms don't CHOOSE to evolve; individuals with EXISTING helpful traits survive and reproduce more; the population's allele frequencies shift over generations; no intentionality is involved; 'organisms develop traits they need' is Lamarckism, which is incorrect

lessons.lessonTitle: The Evidence That Evolution Happened
topics: Fossil record showing change over time
lessons.examTip: Students say 'evolution is just a theory' as if theory means a guess — in science, a THEORY is an explanation supported by extensive evidence and testing; scientific theories explain HOW things happen (evolution, gravity, germ theory); a hypothesis is the guess; a theory is the tested explanation

lessons.lessonTitle: How Scientists Organize and Name All Living Things
lessons.examTip: Students say species that look similar must be closely related — convergent evolution produces similar-looking organisms with NO close relationship (dolphins and fish look similar but are not closely related); classification must be based on EVOLUTIONARY HISTORY (genetics), not appearance

lessons.lessonTitle: How Energy Moves Through an Ecosystem
topics: 10% energy transfer rule between trophic levels
lessons.examTip: Students say 50% of energy passes between trophic levels — only about 10% of energy transfers to the next level; 90% is LOST as heat through cellular respiration; this is why food chains are short and why there are more producers than top predators in any ecosystem

lessons.lessonTitle: How Populations Grow and What Controls Their Size
lessons.examTip: Students say populations grow until 'there's no more room' — populations are limited by RESOURCES (food, water, space), PREDATION, and DISEASE, not just physical space; a meadow might have room for more rabbits but not enough food; food is usually the limiting resource before space

lessons.lessonTitle: How Human Activities Change Ecosystems
topics: Habitat destruction as leading cause of species loss
Pollution and its effects on food chains
lessons.examTip: Students list many causes of extinction as equally important — HABITAT DESTRUCTION is the SINGLE LARGEST cause of species extinction globally; pollution, invasive species, and climate change are significant but secondary; when asked to rank causes, habitat loss is the answer

lessons.lessonTitle: What Speed, Velocity, and Acceleration Are (They're Not the Same)
topics: Acceleration: change in velocity, not just speeding up
lessons.examTip: Students say an object isn't accelerating if it's moving at constant speed in a curve — CHANGING DIRECTION is a change in velocity (direction changed), so it IS accelerating; a car going around a circular track at constant speed is constantly accelerating toward the center

lessons.lessonTitle: How to Read Distance-Time and Speed-Time Graphs
lessons.examTip: Students read a horizontal line on a speed-time graph as 'stopped' — a HORIZONTAL LINE on a speed-time graph means CONSTANT SPEED (not zero speed); the object is only stopped if the line is on the x-axis (speed = 0); a flat line at v = 5 m/s means moving steadily at 5 m/s

lessons.lessonTitle: How Gravity Pulls Everything Down the Same Way
topics: Free fall: all objects accelerate at g = 9.8 m/s²
Why mass doesn't affect fall time (ignoring air resistance)
lessons.examTip: Students say heavier objects fall faster — in a VACUUM, all objects fall at the same rate regardless of mass (Galileo's experiment); air resistance makes a feather fall slower than a hammer in atmosphere; on the moon (no air), both hit the ground simultaneously

lessons.lessonTitle: What Work and Power Mean in Physics (Not in Life)
topics: Work = force × distance in direction of force
Zero work: perpendicular force or no movement
lessons.examTip: Students say holding a heavy box is 'hard work' in physics — physics work requires DISPLACEMENT in the direction of force; holding a box with no movement does ZERO WORK no matter how tiring it is; work requires both force AND movement in the force's direction

lessons.lessonTitle: How Kinetic and Potential Energy Trade Off in Moving Objects
topics: Energy transformations on a roller coaster or pendulum
lessons.examTip: Students say a roller coaster has the most speed at the highest point — speed is maximum at the LOWEST point where KE is maximum (all PE converted to KE); at the highest point, PE is maximum and KE is minimum; height and speed are inversely related in a frictionless system

lessons.lessonTitle: Why Energy Is Never Actually Lost (It Just Changes Form)
topics: Thermal energy as the destination of 'lost' energy
Efficiency: useful energy output vs. total input
lessons.examTip: Students say friction 'destroys' energy — friction CONVERTS mechanical energy to THERMAL energy; total energy is conserved; the energy isn't gone, it's just in a less useful form; efficiency measures how much of the input energy becomes useful output

lessons.lessonTitle: What Waves Actually Are and How They Move
topics: Wave speed, frequency, wavelength: v = fλ
Amplitude and energy: more amplitude = more energy
lessons.examTip: Students say faster waves have higher frequency — wave speed, frequency, and wavelength are related by v = fλ; if SPEED increases and frequency stays the same, WAVELENGTH increases; only frequency changes if you change the source, not the medium; medium changes speed and wavelength together

lessons.lessonTitle: How Light Behaves When It Hits Different Materials
topics: Reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection
Refraction: light bends when changing medium
Total internal reflection and critical angle
lessons.examTip: Students say light bends TOWARD normal when going from fast to slow medium — light bends TOWARD the normal when entering a denser medium (slowing down); it bends AWAY when entering a less dense medium (speeding up); this is why a straw appears bent in water

lessons.lessonTitle: Why White Light Contains All Colors
topics: Visible light: ROY G BIV and frequency order
lessons.examTip: Students say red light has the highest frequency — RED has the LOWEST frequency and LONGEST wavelength in visible light; VIOLET has the highest frequency and shortest wavelength; energy increases with frequency: gamma rays have more energy than radio waves

lessons.lessonTitle: What Electric Charge Is and How It Creates Force
topics: Positive and negative charges; like charges repel
lessons.examTip: Students say only electrons move when charging objects — in solids, only ELECTRONS (negative charges) move; protons are fixed in the nucleus; when a rod becomes positively charged, it LOST electrons, not GAINED protons; charging is always about electron transfer in solids

lessons.lessonTitle: How Voltage, Current, and Resistance Work Together (Ohm's Law)
topics: Voltage (V) = electric pressure; current (I) = flow rate
lessons.examTip: Students say higher voltage always means higher current — current depends on BOTH voltage and resistance: I = V/R; doubling voltage while also doubling resistance keeps current the SAME; you must consider both before predicting what happens to current

lessons.lessonTitle: What Happens to Current and Voltage in Series vs. Parallel Circuits
topics: Series: same current everywhere, voltage divides
Parallel: same voltage across branches, current divides
Why parallel is used in home wiring
lessons.examTip: Students say voltage divides in parallel circuits — in PARALLEL, each branch has the SAME voltage as the source; voltage DIVIDES in SERIES; this is why household circuits are parallel: every device gets the full voltage regardless of how many devices are on
